Q: I'm getting the error The asset "./components/index.jsx.js" is not present in the asset pipeline A:

The issue is that Rails is treating components/index.jsx as the logical asset name and then appending .js, so it ends up looking for:

components/index.jsx.js

The source file itself is fine:

app/javascript/components/index.jsx

The problem is this:

<%= javascript_include_tag 'components/index.jsx' %>

You should reference the compiled JavaScript asset without the .jsx extension:

<%= javascript_include_tag 'components/index', defer: true %>

I'd also change the esbuild command slightly. You're currently using:

"build": "esbuild app/javascript/*.* --bundle --sourcemap --outdir=app/assets/builds --public-path=assets --loader:.js=jsx --platform=node"

Since this is browser-side code, --platform=browser is more appropriate, and you should explicitly handle .jsx files:

"build": "esbuild app/javascript/**/*.{js,jsx} --bundle --sourcemap --outdir=app/assets/builds --public-path=/assets --loader:.js=jsx --loader:.jsx=jsx --platform=browser"

The idea is:

app/javascript/components/index.jsx

    ↓

  esbuild

    ↓

app/assets/builds/components/index.js

    ↓

javascript_include_tag 'components/index'

So Rails shouldn't be asked to resolve the .jsx source file directly. It should resolve the .js file generated by esbuild.

Q: Is Ruby's rand() good enough for gambling games? A:

Ruby's default rand uses Mersenne Twister algorithm. The internal state of the PRNG, although moderately large, and not simple to hack, is in theory small enough that just a few dozen values from 1 to 10 would be enough to determine its state, so your concerns are not unfounded. (Update: Evidently the internal state also "leaks" into the values returned, making hacking it even easier)

I would suggest you use SecureRandom, as it will typically use either /dev/urandom or the open-ssl library as a raw source of randomness. One of these is likely available on your target server, and no additional hardware or specialist libraries are required.

You may want to go further and look into modules that harvest entropy from an external source and then mix it using a cryptographic hashing algorithm (to get an even distribution of bit values). The Ruby gem RealRand connects to some services which do this sort of thing. I could not find anything more modern in Ruby though.

If you are concerned with trusting third-party services, and have time to write your own Ruby wrapper, you could also take a look at a USB device like this one that works from electronic noise.

Q: Tkinter custom selectable/deselectable object using ttk.Label A:

Couple of issues in your code:

  1. You're calling select instead of passing it.
self.bind('<ButtonPress-1>', self.select())

Those parentheses run select() during construction and then binds the return value, so clicking does nothing. Drop the parens and give the handler an event parameter like below.

self.bind('<ButtonPress-1>', self.select)

def select(self, event=None):
    ...
  1. Your images are being garbage collected. img is a local, so it dies when __init__ returns. Tk keeps only a name for the image, not a Python reference, so you get a blank space.

Here is your complete corrected code:

class ImgBox(ttk.Label):
    def __init__(self, parent, imgFile):
        super().__init__(parent, style='Selectable.TLabel')
        self.path = imgFile
        self.img = ImageTk.PhotoImage(Image.open(imgFile))
        self.configure(compound='bottom', image=self.img, text=imgFile)
        self.state(['!selected'])
        self.bind('<ButtonPress-1>', self.select)
        imgBoxes.append(self)

    def select(self, event=None):
        if self.instate(['selected']):
            self.state(['!selected'])
        else:
            self.state(['selected'])


def removeImage():
    for box in imgBoxes[:]:
        if box.instate(['selected']):
            files.discard(box.path)
            imgBoxes.remove(box)
            box.destroy()

Q: Use "terra::predict" with a "quantregForest" model and get the standard deviation of predictions A:

I have downloaded your data but was not able to load it. So, I am using example data available with terra R package. To calculate sd, you have to create a custom prediction function like:

library(terra)
library(caret)

logo <- rast(system.file("ex/logo.tif", package="terra"))   
names(logo) <- c("red", "green", "blue")
p <- matrix(c(48, 48, 48, 53, 50, 46, 54, 70, 84, 85, 74, 84, 95, 85, 
              66, 42, 26, 4, 19, 17, 7, 14, 26, 29, 39, 45, 51, 56, 46, 38, 31, 
              22, 34, 60, 70, 73, 63, 46, 43, 28), ncol=2)

a <- matrix(c(22, 33, 64, 85, 92, 94, 59, 27, 30, 64, 60, 33, 31, 9,
              99, 67, 15, 5, 4, 30, 8, 37, 42, 27, 19, 69, 60, 73, 3, 5, 21,
              37, 52, 70, 74, 9, 13, 4, 17, 47), ncol=2)

xy <- rbind(cbind(1, p), cbind(0, a))

# extract predictor values for points
e <- extract(logo, xy[,2:3])

# combine with response (excluding the ID column)
v <- data.frame(cbind(pa=xy[,1], e))

#build a model, here with glm 
model <- train(pa~., data=v, method = "qrf",
               preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv"))

#predict to a raster
mean_rast <- terra::predict(logo, model, na.rm=T, cpkgs="quantregForest")
plot(mean_rast)

# extract the raw qrf model and the preProcess object caret built
qrf_model <- model$finalModel
pp <- model$preProcess   # NULL if you didn't use preProcess, but you did


# custom prediction function for terra::predict
sd_fun <- function(model, data, ...) {
  # apply the same centering/scaling used during training
  if (!is.null(pp)) data <- predict(pp, data)
  predict(qrf_model, data, what = sd)
}

sd_rast <- terra::predict(logo, model, fun = sd_fun, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(sd_rast)

Q: Scipy Stats ttest_1samp Hypothesis Testing For Comparing Previous Performance To Sample A: 
from scipy.stats import ttest_1samp, t as t_dist

for col in strategies:
    s    = df[col].dropna()
    n    = len(s)
    mean = s.mean()
    se   = s.std() / np.sqrt(n)          # standard error

    t_stat, p = ttest_1samp(s, popmean=0)

    # 95% CI — in daily terms, then annualize
    ci_low  = (mean - 1.96 * se) * 252
    ci_high = (mean + 1.96 * se) * 252

    sig = 'YES ✓' if p < 0.05 else 'NO ✗'

    print(f'{col}: t={t_stat:.2f}, p={p:.4f}, sig={sig}')
    print(f'  95% CI annualized: [{ci_low:.3f}, {ci_high:.3f}]')
